newsitem.title: INDIA: India cuts rates, but race to borrow seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: India cuts rates, but race to borrow seen unlikely.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI)'s decision to cut interest rates on Wednesday is unlikely to bring corporates back to banks to borrow or boost flagging economic growth, bankers and analysts said.
The RBI announced a one percentage point cut in the bank rate, the rate at which banks borrow from the central bank, to 10 percent per annum.

India's state run banks are expected to cut their prime lending rates, currently between 14.0-14.5 percent. But most analysts believed the banks are unlikely to match the RBI cut for size and may drop their PLRs by 0.5 percentage point.
However the surprise move by the RBI showed the central bank's sentiments were in tune with the markets, analysts said.

Subra Subramaniam, director at Hoare Govett India said the central bank was seeking to boost demand and provide the right environment for investment after the tax-cutting 1997/98 budget passed in April.
"After all the good news of the budget the RBI is doing its part to get a broad revival going by pushing demand through interest rate cuts," Subramaniam said.
Growth in industrial output slowed to 8.7 percent in 1996 from 11.6 percent in 1995, according to a Asian Development Bank report released in April.
But slowdown in industry may soon be over, Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia said told India Development Forum at a meeting in Paris.
"I am happy to say that there are signs that the industrial slowdown may soon be reversed," Ahluwalia said.
The RBI also announced a one percentage point cut in interest rates on deposits with maturities from 30 days to one year and on rupee export credit.
"It is a welcome move but I do not see it leading to any sharp increase in bank credit offtake," said Sunil Bhandare, advisor to the blue-chip Tata group of companies.
"Reductions in prime rates in the immediate past have not had any impact on bank credit offtake...so we will have to wait and see," Bhandare said.
Leading state-run banks have cut prime lending rates by 150-200 basis points in the last year but borrowing by corporates remains poor and banks are plagued with a problem of excess liquidity.
In the current year, bank deposits have grown by 141.12 billion rupees ($3.94 billion) over the end-March figure to 5,177.07 billion but loans have grown only by 11.41 billion to 2,776.71 billion.
This has led to a sharp increase in bank investments in government securities.
Investments in government securities have increased by 175.78 billion rupees so far in 1997/98 (April-March) against an increase of only 34 billion in the same period last year.
Adverse credit market conditions had been one of the factors behind a slowdown in industrial growth in the second half of 1996/97 (April-March), according to a top civil servant.
Analysts said the RBI move to lower interest rates was essential to ensure the recovery was maintained.
"The RBI is basically signalling it wants interest rates to come down," said an analyst at a leading U.S. investment bank.
"The current problem for the banking industry is not from the supply side -- funds are available in plenty --- but from the demand side."
The analyst said the RBI was trying to boost demand.
"I think a further cut in interest rates by banks will make it unremunerative for people to put money in financial assets...maybe the RBI is trying to boost consumption demand this way," he said.
He however ruled out any sharp cuts in prime lending rates in the immediate future.
"Bank spreads are already under pressure from the fall in interest rates last year. Any fresh reductions will be marginal, a maximum of 50 basis points," he said. ($1.00=35.80 rupees)
